caseno: Writ Petition No. 2293 of 1994 with Writ Petition No. 2261 of 1995
lawyer:
Zainul Abedin with AKM Qaiyum Khan, Advocates ----- For the Petitioners 
Md Bazlur Rahman Chhana, Assistant Attorney-General ----- For the Opposite Parties
parties:
Russel Vegetable Oil Ltd ------ Petitioner
VS
Collector of Customs and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Kazi AT Manowaruddin J: These two Rules have been heard together as the facts are alike and the points of law involved are same and these shall be disposed of by this common Judgment.

2. Facts stated in Writ Petition No. 2293 of 1994 in short, are that the petitioner Russel Vegetable Oil Limited is a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1913, having its registered office at 195, Motijheel Commercial Areas, Dhaka. The petitioner set up an Oil Refinery Industry under 100% Foreign Investment with the approval of the Board of Investment.

3. In course of business the petitioner company obtained an Indent on 22-8-94 (Annexure-B) from Gardener Smith (South-East Asia) Private Limited, 37 Graig Road, Singapore for the import of 3,000 metric tons of Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil and the price quoted in the indent was US $ 585.00 CFFO Chittagong per metric ton, valid for shipment within September, 1994.

4. After obtaining the indent, a Letter of Credit was opened on 5-9-94 through United Commercial Bank Limited for US $ 585000.00 for the import of 1000 metric tons. Thereafter L/C value was increased on September 10, 1994 to US $ 1,579,500.00 for 2,700 metric tons and lastly the amount of L/C was increased to 1,755,000.00 for the import of 3,000 metric tons as per terms and conditions contained in the said Indent.

5. On arrival of the goods the petitioner submitted a Bill of Entry through its clearing agent for the assessment of the Customs Duty on the basis of the C&F value at the rate of US $ 585.00 per metric ton. The Bill of Entry was duly received by the Customs on 31-10-94 under registration number 8909. Thereafter on 28-11-94 the petitioner was directed to declare the value of the said goods at US $ 670.00 per metric ton by way of an endorsement on the back of the B/E which is the impugned order.

In Writ Petition No. 2261 of 1995 the petitioner M/s. Afsar Oil and Vegetable Products Private Limited is a company incorporated under the Companies Act 1913, having its registered office at 77/5, Moulvi Bazar, Dhaka and, is engaged in the business of refining Soyabean Oil.

6. The petitioner company opened LC through Janata Bank Imamganj Corporate Branch, Dhaka for US $ 2, 38,000.00 for the import of 4,000.00 metric ton Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil at a price of US $ 595.00 C&F Free out Chittagong Per metric tons.

7. Out of the said 4000 metric ton, 1800 Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil arrived on board the vessel 'MT Gysa Sprit' and the Petitioner through its clearing agent submitted 4 separate Bills of Entry for 300 metric tons. 500 metric tons, 500 metric tons and 500 metric tons under Bill of Entry receiving numbers being 483, 484, 485 and 486 respectively, all dated 2-1-95 for the assessment for the Customs Duty on the basis of C&F value. But the Customs Authority by its impugned endorsement on the Bill of Entry directed the petitioner to declare the value of the consignment at US $ 635.00 per metric ton which has been challenged by the petitioner.

8. Mr Zainul Abedin, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner placed before us a copy of the SRO issued by the Government of Bangladesh, Ministry of Finance Internal Resources Division (Customs) dated 28-10-93 to show us that Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil falls under the heading No. 15.07, HS Code No. 15.07, 10.10 and the tariff value was US $ 440.00 per metric ton.

9. It is stated in the petition that said Notification dated 28-10-93 was amended by a subsequently SRO dated 9-6-94 wherein the aforesaid items namely, Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil under HS Code No. 15.07, 10.10 was withdrawn from the tariff schedule.

10. Mr Abedin, submits that the International Market gradually went up and at the time when the Indent was obtained, LC opened, the shipment arrived and the Bills of Entry submitted, the price was US $ 585.00 CPFO Chittagong in respect of consignment mentioned in Writ Petition No. 2293 of 1994 and US $ 595.00 CFFO Chittagong per metric ton for consignment covered under Writ Petition No. 2261 of 1995.

11. The Learned Advocate for the petitioner submits' that in the absence of any fixed tariff value for the said imported merchandise, price has to be determined as per provision of Section 25(1) and (2) of the Customs Act, 1969 i.e. the normal price which the imported goods would face at the time the Bill of Entry.is delivered.

12. Md Bazlur Rahman Chhana, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing with the leave of the Court, submits that the petitioner was required to show independent reliable materials apart from the invoice to establish that the invoice value was the normal value prevalent at the time of the submission of the Bill of Entry.

Section 25 of Customs Act runs as follows:

"25 Value of imported and exported goods—

(1) The value of any imported goods shall be taken to be the normal price, that is to say, the price which they would fetch, on the date referred to in section 30 on a sale in open market between a buyer and a seller independent of each other.

(2) The normal price of any imported goods shall be determined on the following assumption namely:

(a) that the goods brought by sea or land are treated as having been delivered to the buyer at the port or place of importation, as the case may be, and that goods brought by air are treated as having been delivered to the buyer at the Airport or place where they are unloaded in Bangladesh or, if the aircraft lands in Bangladesh at some other Airport or place without unloading the goods, at such other Airport or place:

(b) that the seller will bear freight, insurance, commission and all other cost, charges and expenses incidental to the sale and the delivery of the goods at the port, Airport or place which will be included in the normal price:

(c) that the buyer will bear any duties or taxes applicable in'(Bangladesh) which will not be included in the normal price."

Sub-section: 1 clearly provides that the value of the imported goods shall be the normal price that is to say the price which they would fetch at the time of the submission of the Bill of Entry on a sale in open market between the buyer and a seller independent of each other.

13. The price as mentioned in the letter of Credit and the commercial invoice prima-facie shows that the price mentioned in those documents is the market value between the seller and the buyer, in other words, the supplier and the consignee. Therefore as per provision of section 25(1) said invoice price is to be taken to be the normal price unless of course, the Customs Authority proves otherwise. The Customs have no arbitrary right to reject the invoice value. If they do not accept the invoice value they must have sufficient materials to support their action. There is no such material whatsoever which tends to show that the consignment in question has been under invoiced.

14. Admittedly there was no fixed tariff value for the said imported merchandise at the relevant time.

15. Mr Zainul Abedin, the learned Advocate for the petitioner referring to a Memo dated 3-7-94 issued by Customs Valuation Department submits that the Valuation Department without any lawful authority fixed an "indicative" value for the aforesaid goods. The indicative price so fixed (Annexure E) areas follows:

SL No Description of goods Indicative Value Country of origin

1. CDSO $426.00 FO B/Mt on UK

2. CDSO US$ 650.00 FO B/MT on USA

3. SDSO US$ 574.00 FO B/MT on Maleysia Brazil

16. He next submits that as per said "Indicative value" the Customs Authority by its impugned order directed the petitioner of Writ Petition No. 2293; of 1994 to declare the value of the imported merchandise under Bill of Entry Receiving 3903 dated 31st October 1994 at US$ 670.00 per metric ton.

17. And the petitioner of the Writ Petition No. 2261 of 1995 was directed by the Custom to declare the value of its imported merchandise at the price of US$ 635.00 per metric ton.

18. Mr Zainul Abedin the learned Advocate f6r the petitioner submits that there is a provision under section 25(7) for fixing tariff value but there is no provision under the Customs Act or under any other Act for fixing any "indicative value".

Section 25(7) reads as follows:

"Notwithstanding anything contained in this section, the Government may by notification in the official Gazette, fix for the purpose of levying customs duties, tariff values for any goods imported or exported as chargeable with customs duty advalorem:

Provided that any imported or exported goods the declared value of which is higher than of its tariff value fixed under this sub-section shall be chargeable with customs duties on the basis of its declared value."

19. Even if, tariff value is fixed under section 25(7) it has to be notified in the official gazette. Admittedly (Annexure-E) has not been notified in the official Gazette nor there is any other section available in the Customs Act or any other law wherein the Customs Authority or anybody else has been invested with any power to fix up any "indicative value" for any goods for the purpose of levying duty.

20. Md Bazlur Rahman Chhana, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the respondents has submitted that "Indicative value" has been fixed taking into account sufficient material. However, what are the materials relied upon by the Customs Authorities have not been stated either by way of filing an affidavit-in-opposition or verbally by the learned Deputy Attorney-General.

21. Be that as it may, we have no hesitation to hold that the value as fixed under the heading "indicative value" has no place in the Customs Act or in any other Act. Accordingly in the eye of law, Annexure-E has no value. And on the basis of the said indicative value the Customs Authority has no jurisdiction to direct any consignee to declare the value of the Consignment as per "indicative value".

22. Learned Deputy Attorney-General submits that the said "indicative value" as contained in Annexure-E to the Writ Petition has been prepared by the Valuation Department and is an official act which shall be presumed to be valid and lawful under section 114(e) of the Evidence Act. And to find support to his contention he has referred to the case of Mustafa Kamal vs Commissioner of Customs reported, in 52 DLR (AD) 1. More specifically he refers to paragraph 18 of the decision.

Paragraph 17 reads as follows:

"17. Having heard both sides in extenso we are of the view that when a Writ Petition is filed on a blad assertion that the High powered committee arbitrarily and fictitiously raised tariff value without any objective material before it, the High Court Division ought not to rush into issuing a Rule Nisi and stay payment of duties and taxes. It should take notice under section 114(e) of the Evidence Act 1872 and should start with the presumption of regularity in official business. Initially, in the Writ Petition itself, the Writ Petitioner must include some reliable and relevant materials to show that between the last date of fixation of tariff value and the impugned date of fixation of tariff value the international market price of a particular imported item has either gone down or has gone up to an extent which is significantly higher or lower than the impugned fixation of tariff value, according as the writ petitioner's case is. If there are no such materials in the writ petition itself the High Court Division should not entertain the petition and dismiss it in limine."

23. In the above reported case, under the provision of section 25(7) Government fixed up tariff values for certain item and duly notified the tariff value so fixed by notification in the official Gazette in the form of Statutory Regulatory Order: (SRO) being SRO No. 2 of 1996 Cus dated 18-9-96. The said SRO was challenged on the ground that the tariff value fixed for Soda ash-light was not fixed on the basis of sufficient materials.

24. The facts and circumstances of 'the above reported case and the present cases are quite different. There, the Government in the discharge of their duties in accordance with law i.e. as per provision of section 25(7) of the Customs Act. 1969 fixed up tariff value, accordingly their Lordships in the Appellate Division held that the initial presumption of the court would be that the official act has been duly and regularly performed. In such circumstances the onus lies upon the person who challenges that the fixation has not been duly done. However their Lordships in the Appellate Division found that the price was not fixed on the basis or objective information obtained from reliable materials and allowed the appeal against the Commissioner of Customs.

25. In the instant case we have already observed that the fixation of the "indicative value" as contained in (Annexure-E to the petition) could not even be said to be an order passed under the provision of any of the sections of the Customs Act; the Valuation Department of the Customs, if has fixed such "indicative value", has done so without any authority or jurisdiction.

26. The learned Deputy Attorney-General lastly submits that the writ petitions are not maintainable inasmuch as equally efficacious remedy is available under the Customs Act, 1969. And in support of his submission he refers to the case of Mohammed Brothers vs Collector of Customs reported in 48 DLR (AD) 58.

27. The facts and circumstances of the said case and the facts and circumstances of the present case are quite different. In that case the imported consignment was seized, releasable on payment of fine of Tk. 20,000.00 and the duty imposed by the appraiser. It was observed in that case that "The fact that the petitioner has to deposit the full amount of penalty before filing Appeal is not an absolute provision of Customs Act. There are provisions in the said Act itself mitigating the rigour of the said provision. It is only when a provision for appeal in a Statute is attended with an inviolable and non relaxable condition of payment of fine or extra duty in full that it can be said that the petitioner has no equally efficacious remedy."

28. For appeal against imposition of penalty, deposit of penalty amount at the time of preferring appeal may be dispensed with by the appellate authority if the appellate authority finds that it will cause undue hardship to the appellant.

29. In the present case there was no question of preferring appeal against any penalty.

30. Section 193 of the Customs Act provides that any person aggrieved by any decision or order passed by any officer of Customs under the Act not being an order passed under section 82 or 98 may prefer an appeal within three months of the date of such decision or order.

31. And section 194 of the Customs Act deals with other provision of appeal. Section 194 of the Customs Act runs as follows:

"Deposit, pending appeal, of duty demanded or penalty levied—(1) Any person desirous of appealing under section 193 or section 196(A) against any decision or order relating to any duty demanded in respect of goods which have ceased to be under the control of customs authorities or to any penalty levied under this Act shall, at the time of filing his appeal or if is so permitted by the appellate authority at any later stage before the consideration of the appeal, deposit with the appropriate officer the duty demanded or the penalty levied:

Provided that such person may, instead of depositing as aforesaid the entire amount of the penalty, deposit only fifty percent thereof and furnish a guarantee of the balance:

Provided further that where, in any particular case, the appellate authority is of the opinion that the deposit of duty demanded or penalty levied will cause undue hardship to the appellant, it may dispense with such deposit either unconditionally or subject to such conditions as it may deem fit to impose.

(2) If upon an appeal it is decided that the Whole or any portion of the aforesaid duty was not leviable, the appropriate officer shall return to the appellant such amount or portion as the case may be."

32. It appears from section 194 that the provision of this section is limited and confined to "goods which have ceased to be under the control of the Customs authorities or to any penalty levied under this Act." In other words so long the goods remain in the custody or control of the customs authority, the consignee cannot take the delivery of the goods imported unless the duties demanded by the customs are fully paid no matter whether any appeal has been preferred or not. If any appeal is preferred against the order of any Customs officer in respect of goods which are in the custody of the Customs, there is no provision for ad interim or interim relief. The appellant is to wait till the disposal of the appeal, in the meantime the imported merchandise may he incurring huge port demurrage. So in such cases including the instant case the provision of appeal under the Act can not be said to be an equally efficacious as that of writ.

33. Further we may profitably refer to the case of Collector of Customs, Chittagong and others vs Ahmed Hossain and 39 others reported in 48 DLR (AD) 199. In that case at the time of the opening of the letter of Credit the rate of duty was not less than it was at the time of submission of the Bill of Entry. The consignees were directed to pay customs duty as was prevalent at the time of submission of Bills of Entry. The learned Additional Attorney-General who appeared on behalf of the Collector of Customs in that case, relying upon a decision of another case reported in 48 DLR (AD) 58 submitted that the High Court Division was wrong in holding that the writ petition was maintainable. But their Lordships in the Appellate Division in deciding the case of Collector of Customs Chittagong vs Ahmed Hossain 48 DLR (AD) 199 observed that:

"It has been noticed that the High Court Division in holding as above relied on another decision of this Division 11 BLD (AD) 227. In that decision it has been, inter-alia, observed that in principle where an alternative statutory remedy is available an application under article 102 may not be entertained to circumvent a statutory procedure. But in certain circumstances as mentioned therein the principle may be relaxed. The decision referred to by the learned Additional Attorney-General has not deviated from the principle as above. In the facts of that case it was held that the petitioner had efficacious remedy by way of an appeal under the Customs Act. When in the case of A Hannan this Division found the writ petition to be maintainable. The questions involved in the present writ-petitions being the same as in A Hannan's case, they could not he said to be not maintainable."

34. Following the principles laid down in the decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Collector of Customs, Chittagong and others vs Ahmed Hossain and 39 others, 48 DLR (AD) 195 and the fact that the provisions of section 194 of the Customs Act, 1969 are applicable only to those cases where duty demanded relates to goods "which have ceased to be under the control of Customs authorities" the present petition is held to be maintainable more so for the fact that at the relevant time the imported goods were under the control and custody of the Customs.

35. From the discussion made above we find that the petitioners are liable to pay duties and other charges in respect of their imported merchandise as per their invoice value.

36. In the result, both the Rules are made absolute.

37. The impugned directions as given on the back of the Bills of lading, directing the petitioners to declare higher value are declared to have been passed without any lawful authority.

38. In order to release the consignment imported under letter of credit No. UC BK 235-94 dated 5-9-94 and as declared in bill of entry No. 8909 dated 31-10-94 if the petitioner of Writ Petition No. 2293 of 1994 has furnished any Bank Guarantee to the Customs to cover the difference of ditties and other charges computed on the basis of invoice value of US $ 585.00 per metric ton, and duties and charges, computed on the basis of US $ 670.00 per metric ton as demanded by the Customs such Bank Guarantee be returned to the petitioner M/s Russel Vegetable Oil Ltd the petitioner of Writ Petition No. 2293 of 1994 within two months.

39. There shall be no order as to costs.

Let a copy of this order be sent to the Commissioner of Customs, Chittagong.

End.
